MC-MKE: A Fine-Grained Multimodal Knowledge Editing Benchmark Emphasizing Modality Consistency

Junzhe Zhang, Huixuan Zhang, Xunjian Yin, Baizhou Huang, Xu Zhang, Xinyu Hu, Xiaojun Wan

Paper ↗Code ↗

Correcting one multimodal answer does not ensure related answers change consistently; MC-MKE checks whether edits agree across image recognition, textual facts, and questions about images.

01 / The research question

One edited answer can hide a contradiction

A multimodal model may recognize a person in an image, know which club that person plays for, and answer a club question about the image. These are three related behaviors, not interchangeable copies of one fact. An edit can repair the requested answer while leaving the other two inconsistent. MC-MKE makes their relationship part of the evaluation instead of counting the edited response alone.

The paper’s own example shows why the scenarios differ. A photograph of Messi is misrecognized as Mac Allister, so the model answers that the pictured player plays for Liverpool. Correcting the recognition should also change the image-based club answer to Miami FC, because the textual fact about Messi already supplies it. If instead the club itself changed through a transfer, the recognition should stay fixed while both club answers change. The two interventions can produce the same surface answer for different reasons.

Selected method

FT(LLM) on IE_edit, InstructBLIP: reliability 98.48, consistency 9.09, locality 0.03. The edited answer appears on 98.48% of edit inputs, but the linked answer follows on only 9.09%.

Example: Figure 2 and Section 3.3, described in text. Measured: Appendix E, Tables 9–11 (InstructBLIP with Vicuna-7B; MiniGPT-v2 with Llama-2-Chat-7B). Reliability is scored on the edit input, consistency on the linked probe, locality on five unrelated instances per edit, and generality on five paraphrases or five other images per edit (Section 4.2). The per-method numbers are benchmark averages, not model outputs for the Messi example.

03 / Inside the method

The reason for an edit determines its consequences

The benchmark decomposes multimodal knowledge into an image-to-entity association and an entity–relation–object fact. Their composition produces the image–relation–object answer. It then defines three editing settings: change recognition, change a textual fact, or directly change the multimodal answer. Each setting specifies a different related answer that must be checked for consistency after editing.

The third setting contains an ambiguity: a changed image answer could come from recognizing a different entity or updating a fact about the original one. MC-MKE supplies a reason for the edit, such as a club transfer. In its constructed dataset, this setting is restricted to the textual-fact interpretation. That is a deliberate experimental choice, not a claim that every real multimodal correction has a unique explanation.

Before creating edits, the authors retain source examples only when all three knowledge questions are correctly answered by the three tested multimodal models. Otherwise, a failed consistency check could reflect a missing prerequisite rather than damage from editing. Evaluation then separates reliability on the requested change, consistency of related answers, locality of unrelated knowledge, and generality across alternate images or paraphrases.

  1. 01

    Decompose the knowledge

    Represent image recognition, textual facts, and image-based factual questions as connected components rather than one undifferentiated answer.

  2. 02

    Edit each component

    Construct three editing scenarios and select facts the model can answer across all components before an edit.

  3. 03

    Check the consequences

    Evaluate consistency alongside edit success, generalization to new inputs, and preservation of unrelated knowledge.

04 / Reading the evidence

Consistency must be read alongside locality

  • 44,118

    Test inputs

    The benchmark expands 2,884 knowledge entries into multiple probes, allowing an edit's downstream consistency to be checked from different inputs.

  • Consistency gap

    Across four methods

    Fine-tuning, MEND, IKE, and SERAC do not maintain strong consistency across all three scenarios, especially after image-recognition edits.

The experiments compare fine-tuning, MEND, IKE, and SERAC on InstructBLIP and MiniGPT-v2; LLaVA-v1.5 is used only when selecting the source examples. Strong edit reliability does not reliably imply strong cross-modal consistency. The component being changed also matters: editing visual components is more suitable for some recognition changes, whereas changes to textual facts benefit from access to language components. These are empirical patterns in the tested architectures, not a universal map of where every fact resides.

A second trap is a method that repeatedly outputs the new target. It can appear consistent simply because every related prompt receives the same answer, while unrelated knowledge is damaged. This is why the paper reports several dimensions rather than declaring a winner from one score. The interactive comparison places every method’s measured reliability against its consistency for each scenario and model, using Tables 9–11.

Research summary

MC-MKE evaluates whether multimodal knowledge edits remain consistent across image recognition, textual facts, and image-based factual questions. It introduces three editing scenarios derived from a decomposed representation of multimodal knowledge, and evaluates consistency alongside reliability, locality, and generality. Experiments with fine-tuning, MEND, IKE, and SERAC reveal limitations across the scenarios, particularly in maintaining agreement between related answers after an edit.
